title: Chapter 46: The Beguiling Boy 1
content:
Chapter 46

The Beguiling Boy 1

The smile froze on Wei Wuxian’s lips as if someone had dumped a bucket of ice water right over his head.

The hulking silhouette stood beneath the dead tree, facing dead-on in his direction. If a head were perched on those broad shoulders, it would be staring him down right now.

Over by the bonfire, the Lan juniors caught sight of the figure too. Every single hair on their arms stood on end. Eyes wide with panic, they went to yank their swords, but Wei Wuxian raised an index finger to his lips, cutting the air with a razor-thin "Shh."

He gave them a firm shake of his head, eyes screaming don’t you dare. Catching the cue, Lan Sizhui reached over with noiseless precision, pressing Lan Jingyi’s half-drawn blade right back into its scabbard.

The headless man reached out, resting a massive hand against a withered trunk. He traced the bark for several beats, seemingly turning something over in his mind—or perhaps confirming what the hell he was touching.

He shuffled half a step forward, allowing the faint moonlight to wash over his torso.

The tattered burial shroud draped across his frame was unmistakable. It was the exact same funerary garment on the torso they’d exhumed back in the Chang clan graveyard.

Scattered around his boots lay a mess of shredded fabric: the torn remains of several Qiankun pouches of evil-sealing.

Wei Wuxian winced inwardly. Careless. The good brother actually stitched himself back together!

Come to think of it, between the nonstop circus in Yi City and the madness since, he and Lan Wangji hadn't played Rest together in over two days. Over the trek to Tanzhou, they’d only barely kept the resentful energy on a leash. Now that all four limbs had been reassembled, the physical attraction between the severed pieces had spiked. Choked with centuries of suffocating malice, the parts had hungered to become whole again; the second Lan Wangji stepped away on patrol, they’d seized the opening, burst clean through the enchanted seals, and snapped back together on their own.

Only, the corpse was still missing a piece. The most important one.

The headless figure raised a hand to his neck, his fingers wandering over the clean, scarlet wound sheared across his throat. He felt around, hunting frantically for the head that was supposed to be there. Greeted by empty air, pure rage seemed to detonate in his chest; with a vicious snarl of raw kinetic force, his palm slammed into the tree beside him.

The trunk splintered straight through. Wei Wuxian raised a brow. Lively temper on this guy.

Lan Jingyi brought his scabbard up like a shield, his voice shaking: "W-what kind of monster is that?!"

Wei Wuxian clicked his tongue. "And that's why you need to review your fundamentals. What’s a monster? What’s a demon? This is clearly a corpse, meaning it falls under the ghost classification. How could it be a monster?"

Sizhui whispered nervously, "Senior... talking that loudly, aren't you afraid he'll hear you?"

"Relax," Wei Wuxian replied breezily. "I just realized it doesn't matter how loud we get. He doesn't have a head. No eyes, no ears—he can't see us, and he can't hear us. Go ahead, yell a bit if you don't believe me."

Jingyi blinked. "Really? Let me try."

True to form, he immediately belted out two loud shouts. The second the noise left his mouth, the headless titan wheeled around, stomping straight toward the disciples!

The boys nearly jumped out of their skins. Jingyi shrieked, "You said it didn't matter!"

Wei Wuxian cupped his hands around his mouth, hollering back, "I said the noise didn't matter! Look at me, I’m yelling at the top of my lungs and he isn't looking my way! But your side has a blazing fire! Heat! A cluster of living bodies, and all of you are boys—dripping with concentrated yang energy! He's blind and deaf, sure, but he tracks warmth like a bloodhound! Douse the damn fire and scatter!"

Sizhui swept his sleeve, kicking up a gust of wind that snuffed the flames out cold. In a heartbeat, the flock of disciples bolted in every direction across the overgrown garden.

Sure enough, with the bonfire out and the cluster broken up, the headless man lost his bearing.

He froze in place, standing motionless like a monument. Just as everyone began to exhale, he pivoted on his heel and marched straight toward one of the hiding disciples with chilling accuracy!

Jingyi was on the verge of tears. "You said dousing the fire would work!"

Wei Wuxian didn't have the breath to trade barbs. "Freeze!" he snapped at the targeted boy.

Kicking a loose pebble into his palm, Wei Wuxian flicked his wrist, hurling the stone straight into the titan’s spine. The pebble struck with a sharp clack. The headless man halted, turning his broad shoulders around. Weighing the disturbance, he clearly decided the flying projectile was the bigger threat, rerouting his heavy strides toward Wei Wuxian.

Wei Wuxian drifted two agonizingly slow steps to the left, letting the towering corpse brush past him by an arm’s length. "I told you to scatter, not sprint around like headless chickens," he chided in a hushed, even tone. "Keep your pace slow. This corpse was an elite cultivator in life; move too fast and the draft you kick up will give you away in a heartbeat."

Sizhui whispered from the shadows, "He seems to be feeling around for something... Is he looking for his... head?"

"Spot on," Wei Wuxian said. "He’s hunting for his missing skull. There are plenty of heads attached to shoulders around here; since he doesn't know which one belongs to him, he’ll just twist yours off your necks one by one, screw it onto his own stump, and see if the fit is snug. If it works, he’ll wear it for a while; if it doesn't, he’ll toss it aside and try the next. So walk slow, dodge quiet, and don't let him get his claws on you."

Visualizing their own skulls getting violently wrenched off their necks and jammed onto a bloody, mangled stump, a wave of pure nausea washed over the disciples. In unison, every boy clamped both hands securely around his throat, tip-toeing across the ruined garden in the slowest, most agonizing game of evasion imaginable. It was a deadly game of blind man's bluff: get tagged by the ghost, and your head was his prize. Whenever the headless titan homed in on a boy's draft, Wei Wuxian casually flicked a pebble at his back, drawing the threat straight back onto himself.

Hands tucked behind his back, Wei Wuxian paced with leisurely grace, studying the corpse's every twitch. His posture is bizarre, he thought, watching the figure march. His fist stays half-clenched, swinging his arm in broad, violent arcs... What kind of form is that?

While he turned the mystery over, Lan Jingyi’s patience broke. "Are we seriously just going to wander in circles all night?! How long do we have to keep this up?!"

Wei Wuxian paused, humoring him. "Naturally, we aren't."

He drew in a deep breath and hollered into the night sky: "Hanguang-jun! Hanguang-juuun! Are you back yet?! Save us!"

Taking the cue, the juniors chimed in at the top of their lungs. Since the corpse was entirely deaf, they screamed with reckless abandon, each voice pitching higher and more pathetic than the last. In the middle of their chorus, a low, haunting melody from a jade xiao pierced the gloom, answered a beat later by the crystalline, resonant ring of a zither.

Hearing that twin harmony, the boys practically wept with relief. "Hanguang-jun! Ze-wu-jun!"

Framed by the garden's crumbling stone archway, two tall silhouettes materialized in the moonlight. Both cut figures of peerless, snow-white elegance—one holding a jade xiao, the other bearing a guqin slung across his back, walking shoulder to shoulder. The moment their eyes landed on the headless figure, both stopped dead in their tracks.

Lan Xichen’s reaction was immediate—his composure shattering into raw, naked shock. The xiao, Liebing, went silent, but Bichen was already clearing its scabbard. Sensing the lethal frost surging toward him, the headless titan threw his arm out in a savage swing. Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed. That motion again!

The headless corpse moved with terrifying agility. Vaulting into the air, he slipped past Bichen’s whistling edge, whipped his hand around, and clamped his bare fingers down squarely around Bichen’s hilt!

He hoisted the sword high overhead, angling it as if trying to scrutinize what he had just intercepted—though having no eyes, the gesture was purely instinctual. Watching a corpse catch Hanguang-jun’s personal blade bare-handed drained the color from the disciples' faces. Lan Wangji, however, didn't flinch. In a fluid motion, he summoned his guqin, plucking a single string; the note whipped through the air like an invisible, spinning javelin aimed straight for the corpse’s chest. The headless man slashed Bichen downward, shattering the sonic blade into dust. Lan Wangji swept his hand across all seven strings at once, unleashing a deafening crescendo, while Wei Wuxian brought his bamboo flute to his lips to answer, raining down a storm of whistling, jagged notes!

The headless corpse raised the sword to parry the onslaught. By then, Lan Xichen had shaken off his daze, lifting Liebing back to his lips with furrowed brows. The moment that tranquil, melancholic melody drifted into the air, the corpse’s violent frenzy froze in its tracks. He stood motionless, seemingly listening to the tune, before turning toward the musician. But lacking eyes and a skull, he couldn't process the scene. Hemmed in by the crushing tripartite harmony of xiao, guqin, and flute, the dark energy animating his limbs sputtered out. His massive frame swayed once, then dropped to the dirt.

More accurately, he didn't just drop—he fell apart. Hands, legs, and torso detached, scattering across the rotting leaves like dismantled armor.

Lan Wangji stowed his guqin and called Bichen back to its sheath, walking with Wei Wuxian toward the severed limbs. Inspecting the pile, he produced five fresh Qiankun pouches. The shaken disciples hurried over, formally bowing to Ze-wu-jun; before their frantic babbling could erupt, Lan Wangji dropped a flat verdict: "Rest."

Lan Jingyi blinked in confusion. "Huh? But Hanguang-jun, it's not even nine yet!"

Lan Sizhui gave his sleeve a firm tug, bowing low. "Understood." Taking the hint without a single question, he herded the rest of the flock toward another corner of the courtyard to rekindle a fire and bed down.

With only the three of them left beside the carnage, Wei Wuxian dipped his head in greeting to Lan Xichen, crouched down, and began stuffing the left arm back into an enchanted pouch. He had it halfway in when Lan Xichen’s voice cut through the quiet: "Please, hold on."

Wei Wuxian had clocked the man's expression earlier and knew something was up. Sure enough, Lan Xichen’s face was ashen. He repeated softly, "Please... wait. Let me see the remains."

Freezing his hands, Wei Wuxian asked, "Does Ze-wu-jun recognize this person?"

Lan Xichen hesitated, looking agonizingly conflicted, but Lan Wangji gave a slow, deliberate nod.

Wei Wuxian let out a low breath. "Right. I know who it is now, too."

He dropped his voice to a whisper: "Chifeng-zun... isn't he?"

Back during their high-stakes game of hide-and-seek, the corpse had repeated one specific motion over and over: curled fist, arm swinging in brutal horizontal chops and vertical cleaves. It was the distinct muscle memory of someone swinging a heavy weapon.

Naturally, most would assume a sword. But Wei Wuxian was a swordsman himself, having crossed blades with countless masters across the sects, and he had never seen anyone wield a sword like that. The sword was the gentleman of weapons; its forms demanded a degree of poise, balance, and flowing grace. Even an assassin's blade carried a thread of agile finesse beneath its venom. True swordplay leaned heavily on thrusts, parries, and flicks, rarely ever resorting to blunt hacking and cleaving. That headless corpse swung with crushing, violent weight—reeking of pure battlefield slaughter, totally stripped of elegance.

Yet, if the weapon in his grip wasn't a sword, but a saber—a massive, brutally heavy saber built for absolute carnage—the puzzle pieces clicked together.

A saber and a sword walked entirely different paths. In life, this man’s signature weapon had to be a saber. His forms were designed purely for crushing momentum, not dainty decorum. While hunting for his head, he had also been hunting for his blade. That was why he’d kept repeating the hacking motions, and why he’d seized Bichen only to swing it like a broadsword.

Before tonight, the dismembered parts bore no distinct birthmarks, and having been hacked to pieces, identifying the corpse had been impossible. Nie Huaisang hadn't recognized it in the Saber Tomb, and frankly, Wei Wuxian couldn't guarantee he’d recognize his own severed leg if someone tossed it at his feet. Only when the limbs temporarily fused back onto the torso did the towering silhouette give the game away to the Twin Jades of Lan.

Wei Wuxian looked up. "Ze-wu-jun, Hanguang-jun briefed you on everything we saw on the road, right? Mo Village, the grave robber, Yi City?"

Lan Xichen nodded.

"Then he must have mentioned that the fog-masked grave robber who tried to snatch the torso at the Chang cemetery knew the Gusu Lan sword forms inside and out," Wei Wuxian pressed. "That leaves only two possibilities: first, he is a disciple of the Lan clan who was drilled on your sword forms since boyhood. Second, he is an outsider who is intimately familiar with your techniques—someone who either spars with Lan masters regularly, or possesses a genius intellect capable of memorizing sword patterns after a single glance."

Lan Xichen remained stone-faced and silent.

Wei Wuxian drove the point home: "He’s stealing the body parts because he cannot let the world discover Chifeng-zun was dismembered. Once the corpse is whole, the truth will destroy him. We are looking for someone who knows the hidden secrets of the Qinghe Nie Saber Tombs, someone who shares an exceptionally intimate bond with the Gusu Lan Sect, and someone with a deep... history with Chifeng-zun."

Who fit that description was painfully obvious; there was no need to say the name out loud.

Yet Lan Xichen’s brow furrowed, his answer swift and unyielding: "He would never do this."

Wei Wuxian raised an eyebrow. "Ze-wu-jun?"

"Your investigation and the encounters with the grave robber all took place this month," Lan Xichen said, his tone tight. "Throughout this entire month, he has been conferring with me late into the night. Just days ago, we were finalizing the logistics for the upcoming Discussion Conference at Carp Tower. He was completely occupied; it is impossible for him to be the grave robber."

Wei Wuxian countered, "What if he used a Teleportation Talisman?"

Lan Xichen shook his head, his gentle voice carrying an absolute, razor-sharp certainty: "Teleportation talismans require mastery over advanced spatial arts—a discipline that is notoriously grueling to cultivate, and one he has never shown the slightest aptitude for. Furthermore, activating such an art drains a monstrous amount of spiritual energy. Yet he and I went night-hunting together recently, and his spiritual output was immaculate. I am certain he has never used a teleportation talisman."

Lan Wangji spoke up quietly: "He did not need to go in person."

Lan Xichen simply shook his head again, refusing to yield.

Wei Wuxian looked at him directly. "Sect Leader Lan, deep down, you know exactly who the prime suspect is. You simply refuse to accept it."

The flickering embers of the distant fire cast shifting, dancing shadows across their faces. The overgrown garden sank into suffocating silence.

After a long while, Lan Xichen murmured softly, "I know that for various reasons, the world harbors endless prejudice against him. But... I only believe what my own eyes have witnessed over all these years. I know his character. He is not that kind of man."

It wasn't hard to see why Lan Xichen was defending him. To be completely fair, Wei Wuxian’s own impression of their prime suspect wasn't terrible either. Perhaps due to his humble origins, the man carried himself with disarming humility, possessing the rare gift of never stepping on anyone's toes—making everyone around him feel comfortable and respected. If a total stranger felt that warmth, what of Lan Xichen, who had shared a close brotherhood with him for years?

Back when Nie Mingjue was alive, the Qinghe Nie Sect had reached the absolute peak of its power under his iron fist, directly rivaling the prestige of the Lanling Jin Sect. Who benefited the most from his death?

Suffering a violent qi deviation in front of the entire cultivation world—a tragic, unavoidable misfortune on the surface. But was the truth really that simple?
